lessons.title: Short Questions
lessons.notes_html:
(i) How does breathing differ from respiration?

Breathing is the physical process of moving air in and out of the lungs (ventilation): it is simply the exchange of gases between the body and the environment. Respiration is the whole biochemical process by which cells break down glucose with oxygen to release energy (ATP), producing carbon dioxide and water. Breathing is one step that supplies oxygen for respiration; respiration itself takes place inside the cells.

(ii) How much carbon dioxide is present in venous and arterial blood?

Venous blood (returning to the heart and lungs) contains more carbon dioxide, about 53 ml per 100 ml of blood, carried mainly as bicarbonate. Arterial blood (leaving the lungs) contains less carbon dioxide, about 48 ml per 100 ml of blood, because carbon dioxide is released in the lungs during expiration. The difference (about 5 ml per 100 ml) is the carbon dioxide removed in one passage through the lungs.

(iii) How does air always remain in the lungs of human beings?

Air always remains in the lungs because even after a forced expiration, a volume of air (the residual volume, about 1200 ml) stays in the lungs and cannot be expelled. This happens because the lungs are elastic but are held open inside the chest, and the small airways close before all the air can leave. The residual air keeps the alveoli open and lets gas exchange continue between breaths.

(iv) What are the products which are produced during photorespiration?

The products of photorespiration are: carbon dioxide, which is released (so photorespiration wastes fixed carbon); phosphoglycolate, which is processed through the peroxisome and mitochondrion to form glycine and serine, releasing ammonia and another carbon dioxide; and no ATP or NADPH is gained — in fact ATP is used up. Photorespiration is therefore a wasteful process that lowers the efficiency of photosynthesis.

(v) How much denser is a water medium than air medium for exchange of respiratory gases?

Water is about 800 times denser than air, and oxygen diffuses about 10,000 times more slowly in water than in air. Water also holds far less dissolved oxygen than air holds as a gas. That is why aquatic animals must spend much more energy moving water over their gills, and why air is a far better respiratory medium than water.

lessons.title: Extensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
(i) In what ways is air a better respiratory medium than water?

Air is better than water because: it contains about 20 times more oxygen per unit volume; oxygen diffuses about 10,000 times faster in air than in water; air is about 800 times less dense, so moving it over a respiratory surface costs far less energy; and air does not need to be pumped continuously in large volumes. Water breathers must therefore work much harder to obtain the same amount of oxygen.

(ii) What is photorespiration? Give its consequences.

Photorespiration is the process in which the enzyme RuBisCO, instead of fixing carbon dioxide, fixes oxygen onto RuBP, producing phosphoglycolate. Its consequences are all harmful to the plant: fixed carbon is lost as carbon dioxide, ATP and reducing power are wasted, ammonia is released and must be re-fixed, and the rate of photosynthesis falls, especially in hot, dry conditions when stomata close and oxygen builds up inside the leaf.

(iii) Describe briefly the properties of respiratory surfaces in cockroach.

The cockroach breathes through a tracheal system: air enters through spiracles on the body wall and passes through tracheae that branch into fine tracheoles reaching every tissue. The respiratory surfaces (the tracheole walls) are thin, moist and close to the tissues, so gases diffuse directly to the cells without blood transport. The spiracles can open and close to reduce water loss, and body movements help pump air in and out.

(iv) In what ways is respiration in birds the most efficient and elaborate?

Bird respiration is the most efficient because: air flows through the parabronchi in one direction only, and blood flows in the opposite direction (counter-current exchange), so oxygen is taken up along the whole length; the lungs are supplemented by air sacs that store air and keep fresh air flowing through the lungs during both inspiration and expiration; and the thin parabronchial walls give a huge surface. Birds therefore extract more oxygen than mammals, which suits the high energy demand of flight.

(v) Discuss the mechanical aspects of breathing in man.

Breathing in man is driven by changes in chest volume. In inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostal muscles raise the ribs, increasing chest volume; air pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, and air rushes in. In expiration, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax, the chest volume falls, lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure, and air is pushed out. Inspiration is active (uses energy), while quiet expiration is passive.

(vi) Write a detailed note on respiratory pigments.

Respiratory pigments are coloured proteins that carry oxygen (and carbon dioxide) in the blood. The main one in man is haemoglobin, found in red blood cells: each molecule has four haem groups with iron, binds four oxygen molecules in the lungs (where oxygen is high) to form oxyhaemoglobin, and releases them in the tissues (where oxygen is low). Other pigments are myoglobin in muscles (stores oxygen), haemocyanin in some molluscs and crustaceans (copper-based, blue when oxygenated), and haemerythrin in some worms. Without pigments, blood could carry far too little oxygen.

(vii) List the air passage way in sequence from nostrils to alveoli. Describe the structure of alveolus in detail.

The air passageway is: nostrils (external nares) -> nasal cavities -> pharynx -> larynx (voice box) -> trachea (windpipe) -> bronchi (one to each lung) -> bronchioles -> alveolar ducts -> alveolar sacs -> alveoli. An alveolus is a tiny, thin-walled air sac, about 0.2 mm across: its wall is a single layer of flat squamous cells, surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries, with elastic fibres that let it stretch and recoil. The wall is moist, so gases dissolve and diffuse quickly between the air and the blood, and the huge number of alveoli (about 300 million) gives an enormous surface for exchange.

lessons.title: True or False
lessons.notes_html:
(i) The intercellular openings in the blood capillaries are larger than the openings in the lymph capillaries.

Answer: False - Correction: The openings in lymph capillaries are larger than those in blood capillaries: that is how large proteins, bacteria and cell debris can enter the lymph, while blood capillaries keep them out.

(ii) Between the left auricle and the left ventricle in human heart, the valve present is called tricuspid valve.

Answer: False - Correction: The valve between the left auricle (atrium) and the left ventricle is the bicuspid (mitral) valve, with two flaps. The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart, between the right auricle and the right ventricle.

(iii) The pacemaker of the heart of man is the AV node.

Answer: False - Correction: The pacemaker of the human heart is the SA node (sinoatrial node) in the wall of the right auricle, which starts each heartbeat. The AV node only relays the impulse to the ventricles after a short delay.

(iv) Each sieve tube member is associated with one or more tracheid cells.

Answer: False - Correction: Each sieve tube member is associated with one or more companion cells, which are living cells that support the sieve tube member (which has no nucleus). Tracheids are xylem cells for water transport, not phloem companions.

(v) The method of active immunization is used to combat active infections of tetanus and rabies.

Answer: False - Correction: Passive immunization is used to combat an active infection of tetanus or rabies, because ready-made antibodies give immediate protection. Active immunization (vaccination) is preventive: it takes time to build immunity and is given before infection.

lessons.title: Extensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
(i) How are minerals and water taken up by roots? Draw the structures involved and the pathways for water and minerals from soil water to xylem, and the transport processes at each step.

Water and minerals enter the root mainly through the root hairs, by osmosis (water) and diffusion or active transport (minerals). From the root hair they move through the cortex to the xylem by three pathways: the apoplast pathway (through cell walls and intercellular spaces), the symplast pathway (through the cytoplasm and plasmodesmata), and the vacuolar pathway (through cell vacuoles). At the endodermis the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast pathway, forcing water and minerals through the living cells into the symplast, and from there into the xylem. Practical task: draw the root section and label root hair, epidermis, cortex, endodermis, Casparian strip, pericycle and xylem, with arrows for the three pathways.

(ii) Describe the mechanism of opening and closing of stomata.

Stomata open and close by changes in the turgidity of their two guard cells. In light, the guard cells actively take up potassium ions and produce malate, so their solute concentration rises; water enters by osmosis, they become turgid, and because their inner walls are thicker, they bend outward, opening the pore. In darkness or when water is scarce, potassium leaves the guard cells, water follows out, they become flaccid, and the pore closes. Abscisic acid (ABA) also promotes closure during drought.

(iii) How does the pressure-flow theory explain the movement of sugars through a plant?

The pressure-flow (mass flow) theory explains sugar transport in the phloem as follows: sugars are actively loaded into the sieve tubes at the source (such as a leaf), raising the solute concentration, so water enters by osmosis and builds a high pressure. At the sink (such as a root or fruit), sugars are unloaded, water leaves, and the pressure falls. The pressure difference between source and sink drives the sugary sap to flow from source to sink through the sieve tubes.

(iv) Describe cohesion-tension theory of water movement in xylem. What supplies the cohesion, and what is the source of tension? How do these two forces interact to move water through plant?

The cohesion-tension theory says that water is pulled up the xylem by transpiration. The source of tension is transpiration from the leaves: water evaporating from mesophyll cells pulls water from the xylem, creating a negative pressure (tension) that travels down the water column. Cohesion is supplied by hydrogen bonds between water molecules, which hold the water column together, and adhesion holds water to the xylem walls. Together, tension pulls from above and cohesion keeps the column unbroken, so water rises continuously from roots to leaves, even in tall trees.

(v) Explain apoplast, symplast and vacuolar pathways, and describe the movement of water and dissolved minerals, through them.

The apoplast pathway is movement through the non-living parts: cell walls and intercellular spaces, without crossing any membrane; it is fast but is blocked by the Casparian strip at the endodermis. The symplast pathway is movement through the living cytoplasm of cells, connected by plasmodesmata; minerals must cross membranes, often by active transport, to enter it. The vacuolar pathway is movement through the vacuoles of cells, crossing the tonoplast at each cell. Water and minerals usually use a mixture of all three until the endodermis, where they are forced into the symplast.

(vi) Explain water potential. What is the relationship of water potential with solute potential and pressure potential?

Water potential is the tendency of water to move from one place to another, measured in megapascals; water always moves from higher to lower water potential. Pure water at atmospheric pressure has a water potential of zero, and adding solutes or applying pressure changes it. The relationship is: water potential = solute potential + pressure potential. Solute potential is always negative (solutes lower water potential), while pressure potential is usually positive in turgid cells (the wall pressing back) and zero in flaccid cells.

(vii) Name and describe the general functions of the three major type of cells or cell like bodies found in blood of humans. Which of these cell types is found predominantly in lymph?

The three major types are: (1) Red blood cells (erythrocytes): biconcave discs without nuclei, containing haemoglobin, which carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and bring back some carbon dioxide. (2) White blood cells (leukocytes): larger, nucleated cells that defend the body by engulfing germs (phagocytes) and by making antibodies (lymphocytes). (3) Platelets (thrombocytes): small cell fragments that help blood to clot and stop bleeding. White blood cells, especially lymphocytes, are found predominantly in lymph.

(viii) Write a note on immunity and its types.

Immunity is the body's ability to resist and destroy disease-causing germs and foreign substances. Its types are: innate (natural) immunity, present from birth, including the skin, mucus, stomach acid, phagocytes and inflammation; and acquired (adaptive) immunity, developed during life. Acquired immunity is of two kinds: active immunity, produced by the body's own response after infection or vaccination, which is long-lasting; and passive immunity, given by ready-made antibodies from the mother or by injection, which is immediate but short-lived. Artificial active immunity is vaccination; artificial passive immunity is antiserum injection.
